title: "Fine-tuning for classification"

## Transfer learning

Training a transformer from scratch needs huge amounts of data and compute. Instead, we usually start from a model someone else already pretrained, and adapt it to our own, smaller, labelled task.

:::{.incremental}
* **Pretraining**: expensive, general-purpose, done once by someone with a lot of compute (e.g. `Qwen`, BERT).
* **Fine-tuning**: cheap, task-specific, done by us — we're only nudging weights that already encode a lot about language.
:::

## Classification heads

A pretrained encoder produces a representation per token (or per sequence), not a class label. We attach a small, task-specific **classification head** on top — one or two linear layers — and train *that* (and optionally the rest of the model) on labelled examples.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
from transformers import AutoModelForSequenceClassification

model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(
    "distilbert-base-uncased", num_labels=2
)
```

. . .

Everything below the head was pretrained; the head itself starts from random weights and has everything to learn.

The head reads only the output at the first token, `[CLS]`, which serves as a summary of the whole sequence.

## Where the parameters are

```{python}
#| output: asis
from collections import Counter

def part(name):
    if name.startswith("distilbert.embeddings"):
        return "Embeddings (token + position)"
    if ".attention." in name:
        return "Attention ($W_Q, W_K, W_V$, output), 6 layers"
    if ".ffn." in name:
        return "Feed-forward, 6 layers"
    if "layer_norm" in name:
        return "Layer norms"
    return "Classification head"

counts = Counter()
for name, p in model.named_parameters():
    counts[part(name)] += p.numel()
total = sum(counts.values())
print("| Part | Parameters | Share |\n|---|--:|--:|")
for k in ["Embeddings (token + position)", "Attention ($W_Q, W_K, W_V$, output), 6 layers",
          "Feed-forward, 6 layers", "Layer norms", "Classification head"]:
    n = counts[k]
    share = f"{n / total:.1%}" if n / total >= 0.001 else "<0.1%"
    print(f"| {k} | {n:,} | {share} |")
print(f"| **Total** | **{total:,}** | |")
```

. . .

The new head is under 1% of the model. But by default *every* parameter has `requires_grad=True`, so fine-tuning updates all 67 million of them, not just the head.

## Cross-entropy loss

Classification heads are trained with **cross-entropy loss**, which compares the predicted probability distribution (from `softmax`, as before) against the one-hot true label.

$$\mathcal{L} = -\log p_{\text{true class}}$$

```{python}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from numpy import linspace, log

plt.rcParams.update({"font.family": ["Helvetica Neue", "Helvetica", "DejaVu Sans"],
                     "font.size": 13, "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})
RED, BLUE, GREY = "#b8352a", "#2c6fb7", "#999999"

p = linspace(0.005, 1, 400)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3))
ax.plot(p, -log(p), color=RED, lw=2.5)
ax.set_xlim(0, 1); ax.set_ylim(0, 5.5)
ax.set_xlabel(r"$p_{\text{true class}}$")
ax.set_ylabel(r"$\mathcal{L}$", rotation=0, ha="right", va="center")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Train / validation / test splits

:::{.incremental}
* **Train**: what the model's weights are actually updated on.
* **Validation**: used *during* development — to compare models, tune hyperparameters, decide when to stop training. Never used to update weights directly.
* **Test**: touched only once, at the very end, to report a final, unbiased performance number.
:::

. . .

Mixing these up — e.g. tuning based on test performance — lets information leak from data you're supposed to be held out on, and makes your reported numbers optimistic.

## Evaluating a classifier

Accuracy alone can be misleading, especially with imbalanced classes. A **confusion matrix** breaks predictions down by what was predicted vs. what was true:

|                | Predicted positive | Predicted negative |
|----------------|:---:|:---:|
| **Actual positive** | TP | FN |
| **Actual negative** | FP | TN |

:::{.incremental}
* **Precision** $= \frac{TP}{TP+FP}$: of the things we called positive, how many actually were?
* **Recall** $= \frac{TP}{TP+FN}$: of the things that actually were positive, how many did we catch?
* **F1** is the *harmonic mean* of precision and recall.
:::

## Arithmetic vs. harmonic mean

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
def arithmetic_mean(a, b):
    return (a + b) / 2

def harmonic_mean(a, b):
    return 2 * a * b / (a + b)

for a, b in [(0.5, 0.5), (0.9, 0.1)]:
    print(f"({a}, {b}):  arithmetic {arithmetic_mean(a, b):.2f},"
          f"  harmonic {harmonic_mean(a, b):.2f}")
```

. . .

F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall. A classifier that is excellent on one and poor on the other gets no credit for the average: the smaller number dominates.

## Padding and attention masks

A batch needs every sequence to be the same length, but real sequences vary. We pad the short ones out with a `[PAD]` token.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
from transformers import AutoTokenizer

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("distilbert-base-uncased")
tokenizer(["a short one", "a rather longer sentence than that"], padding=True)
```

. . .

Notice the `attention_mask`: `1` for real tokens, `0` for padding. This tells the model to ignore the padding entirely, so it doesn't contaminate the attention computation or the loss.

## Why small classifiers still matter

Even with frontier LLMs, a fine-tuned model of this size is often the right tool: fast, cheap enough to run over billions of items, runnable locally on private data, and it outputs a score rather than free text.

:::{.incremental}
* **Data filtering**: scoring web pages for quality or toxicity before LLM pretraining.
* **Guardrails**: flagging jailbreaks, prompt injection or harmful content.
* **PII detection**: finding names, addresses etc. to redact (token classification).
* **Retrieval**: embeddings for search, and rerankers, in RAG systems.
* **Routing**: deciding which tool or model a request should go to.
* **Reward models**: the same recipe (pretrained LM + scalar head), scaled up, to score chatbot responses.
:::
